You said something last week that stayed with me. You said the quiet was the hardest part. I would have guessed the opposite.
Everybody guesses the opposite. For about a year the silence here was unsettling. I used to put the radio on just to have a voice in the house.
And now?
Now it has grown on me. I am used to hearing nothing after eight, and when I go back to the city I cannot sleep.

That is exactly what happened to me in reverse. I grew up in Mumbai, so I am used to noise the way you are used to silence. My first month here I genuinely thought something was wrong with the building.
What was the hardest thing for you? The culture shock, or the language?
Honestly, neither. It was that everything closes at six. I was completely thrown by that. Three years later I am still getting used to it, and my wife says I never will.
Then we are the same person. It takes some getting used to, and then one day you are the one who finds the other place strange.
I am used to the silence now, but it took a year.

I used to live in a city of twelve million people.
It grew on me, and now I crave it when I am away.
Four time zones in one working day takes some getting used to.

My name is Anjali, and I have been in Manchester for three years now. People always ask about the weather, and the weather was never the problem. What I could not adjust to was how quiet a building is. In Pune, my parents live on the third floor and there are voices on the stairs at every hour, somebody is always cooking, and a horn goes off every forty seconds. It is not pleasant, exactly, but you never feel alone in it. Here my flat is completely silent from nine at night, and for the first year that silence was unsettling. I used to put a video on just to have a voice in the room. What I am used to now is the opposite. I went home in March and I could not sleep for two nights, and my mother found that very funny. So I am not going to tell you that one is better. I am telling you that you can get used to almost anything, and then the thing you came from becomes the strange one.

This is Marcus. I work with a team in four time zones, and the first six months nearly broke me. I am on the east coast, and my colleagues are in Bangalore, Berlin and Sao Paulo, so somebody is always starting their day while somebody else is finishing. In the beginning I answered everything the second it came in, at eleven at night, at six in the morning, and I was completely wrecked by March. What I had to get used to was not the hours. It was letting a message sit. That took me a year, and honestly it still takes effort. The part nobody warns you about is that you also get used to hearing five different Englishes in one meeting, and after a while you stop noticing whose is whose. Somebody joined us last month and said she could not follow the calls at all, and I realized I could not remember what that felt like.
